newsitem.title: ITALY: Supervision for Brcko while future on ice to 1998.
newsitem.headline: Supervision for Brcko while future on ice to 1998.

text.p: A U.S. arbiter ruled on Friday that the volatile Bosnian town of Brcko, claimed by both Serbs and the Moslem-Croat federation, would be put under international supervision pending a final decision next year on its status.

The West's chief representative, Carl Bildt, said the ruling sought to strike a balance in "the mother of all difficulties in the Bosnian peace process" and U.S. envoy John Kornblum welcomed it as "definitely enough" to avert the threat of renewed war.
"No winner is being awarded today," Roberts Owen, chairman of a three-member arbitration panel deciding the town's fate, told a news conference in Rome.
"We want international supervision for Brcko for not less than one year...to allow for a reduction of tensions," he said.
"We will make a final choice no later than March 1998."
Owen said his ruling firmly rejected the status quo in favour of a major international effort to reduce underlying tensions in the area.

But he added that it was "very possible" that Brcko could eventually become a special district of Bosnia-Herzegovina with something like the status of Washington DC. It would thus remain outside exclusive political control of the Bosnian Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
Brcko, a Sava River port considered one of the region's main flashpoints, was captured by Bosnian Serbs early in the 1992-95 war and purged of its mainly Moslem-Croat pre-war population.
Serbs had threatened to resume war if they were denied control of the town, which sits on a narrow land corridor linking eastern and western halves of Serb-controlled territory.
The federation made a counter threat, saying that handing Brcko to the Serbs would reward ethnic cleansing.

Owen said in his 43-page written ruling that the federation's organisational arrangements were too incomplete. The Serbs had shown "almost total disregard" for implementation of the Dayton peace deal in the Brcko area.
Moreover, the joint inter-ethnic institutions which preside over Bosnia's autonomous Serb and Moslem-Croat entities were not yet fully effective.
"We are not yet convinced that any of the three candidates are sufficiently stabilised to take on the situation," he said.

Instead, a new international supervisor would have the job of strengthening democratic institutions and overseeing implementation of the Dayton peace deal that ended Bosnia's war but was almost scuppered by the Brcko dispute.
Bildt, the international community's High Representative for Bosnia, said he would nominate a deputy for the role and had already asked the United States to propose candidates.
The other two members of the arbitration panel representing the Bosnian Serbs and the federation did not sign the final document and Bildt forecast further tough times.
"It's not going to be solved by tonight or by the end of the weekend or this week or one month but in one year's time," he told reporters. "Let's hope...it can be done."
Owen said the supervisor would be empowered to issue regulations to local police "that should produce basic law and order" and set up a multi-ethnic police force "in due course".
The supervisor should ensure full freedom of movement, oversee the return of Moslem-Croat war refugees and implement an economic revitalisation programme for the Brcko area.
The supervisor would also work with the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe to organise local elections.
The Sava River port will be placed under exclusive control of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Transportation Company.
